records.our_prose: Cabbage is a heavy feeder that needs steady nitrogen to build a large, solid head. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson: 5-10-10 at 3 pounds per 100 square feet), then side-dress with nitrogen once the plants are established and again as heads begin to cup, using about 34-0-0 or calcium nitrate. Keep nitrogen steady through heading, but pair it with even moisture: a late surge of growth from heavy feeding plus a sudden drink of water is what splits heads.
records.source_context: In general, if your garden is located on deep, sandy soil, apply a complete preplant fertilizer such as 5-10-10 or 6-12-12 at the rate of 1 to 2 pounds per 100 square feet. If your soil has a high percentage of clay, a fertilizer such as 10-20-10 or 12-24-12 applied at 1 to 2 pounds per 100 square feet should be suitable.

records.our_prose: In cold regions, cabbage is a spring crop and a fall crop. Start seeds indoors and set plants out in spring for a summer harvest, and start a second batch in early-to-mid summer for a fall harvest, when the cool weather makes especially good heads. In the very coldest zones the season is short, so lean on quick early varieties. Keep the watering even so the heads do not crack.

records.our_prose: Across the cold northern tier cabbage is a spring-and-fall double crop. Start transplants under cover and set them out from April (cold zones) to March (mild end) for a late-spring to midsummer harvest, then set a second crop in mid-to-late summer for a fall harvest that runs into November and, at the mild end, December. The coolest zones (3 to 5) crop through a moderate summer with no real heat gap; the warmer zones (6 to 7) reach genuine midsummer heat that excludes heading, so those calendars carry a backed summer pause. Quick early varieties suit short seasons and the fall crop; late storage types want the long fall window. Harvest months are derived from the sourced planting windows plus the crop's 60-to-120-day maturity.

records.our_prose: In the warm-arid high desert (El Paso and similar zone-8 areas), grow cabbage as a late-winter spring crop and a late-summer fall crop. NMSU lists cabbage as hardy, planted as soon as the ground can be worked in spring or in midsummer for the fall garden; Texas A&M gives spring 4 to 6 weeks before the frost-free date and fall 10 to 16 weeks before the first freeze. The exact month tables are in PDF/complex sources that did not parse, so the planting window is modeled on those rules. Harvest months derived.
